questions.q: Intersectionality emphasizes that:
o: Overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class produce distinct experiences of oppression
Correct: Intersectionality (Crenshaw) holds that overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class interact to produce distinct experiences of oppression.
Each form of inequality operates independently
Independent operation of each inequality denies the interaction central to the concept.
Inequality is mainly economic
Inequality being mainly economic ignores multiple interacting categories.
Race is biologically determined
Race being biologically determined contradicts the social-construction view.
questions.x: Intersectionality (Crenshaw) holds that overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class interact to produce distinct experiences of oppression. Trap: Treating each category as additive.

questions.q: Marx's concept of alienation describes workers' estrangement from:
o: Their families
Families are not the focus of Marx's alienation.
Their government
Government is not what workers are alienated from in his concept.
Their labor, products, and fellow workers
Correct: Marx's alienation describes workers' estrangement from their labor, the products they make, fellow workers, and their human potential, from lack of control over work.
Cultural norms
Cultural norms estrangement is closer to anomie.
questions.x: Marx's alienation describes workers' estrangement from their labor, the products they make, fellow workers, and their human potential, from lack of control over work. Trap: Treating alienation as a purely psychological mood rather than a result of the economic structure of work.

questions.q: Which factor best explains class-based gaps in educational achievement according to most sociologists?
o: Fixed differences in innate ability between classes
Class-linked innate ability is not supported by evidence.
Lower value placed on education by poor families
Poor families do value education, so lower valuation is not supported.
Differences in the age at which children start school
School start age does not explain class-based gaps.
Unequal school funding and family resources
Correct: Unequal school funding and family resources create structural advantages that most sociologists see as the main source of class gaps in achievement.
questions.x: Unequal school funding and family resources create structural advantages that most sociologists see as the main source of class gaps in achievement. Trap: Blaming individual or cultural deficits rather than structural resource differences.

questions.q: Which event of meiosis is responsible for reducing the chromosome number from diploid to haploid?
o: Separation of sister chromatids during anaphase II
Sister chromatid separation in anaphase II leaves ploidy unchanged (haploid to haploid).
Replication of DNA during the S phase preceding meiosis
DNA replication in S phase doubles DNA content and does not alter chromosome number.
Exchange of segments between homologs during prophase I
Crossing over rearranges alleles between homologs without changing chromosome number.
Separation of homologous chromosomes during anaphase I
Correct: In anaphase I each homolog (still two chromatids) moves to an opposite pole, so each daughter cell receives one chromosome of each pair, halving ploidy.
questions.x: In anaphase I each homolog (still two chromatids) moves to an opposite pole, so each daughter cell receives one chromosome of each pair, halving ploidy. Trap: Thinking that sister chromatid separation, the step that resembles mitosis, is what halves ploidy.

questions.q: Failure of one homologous pair to separate during meiosis I (and no other errors) is expected to produce which set of gametes from that cell?
o: Four aneuploid gametes: two with n+1 and two with n-1
Correct: Both homologs move to one pole in meiosis I, so both secondary cells are abnormal and all four products are aneuploid (two n+1, two n-1).
Two normal gametes and two aneuploid gametes
Two normal and two aneuploid gametes is the result of nondisjunction in meiosis II, where only one secondary cell is affected.
Four normal haploid gametes
All four gametes normal would need no error at all.
Two n+1 gametes and two normal gametes
N-1 gametes also form, so two n+1 and two normal is incomplete and wrong.
questions.x: Both homologs move to one pole in meiosis I, so both secondary cells are abnormal and all four products are aneuploid (two n+1, two n-1). Trap: Confusing the outcomes of meiosis I and meiosis II nondisjunction.

questions.q: A small group of birds colonizes an island, and a rare allele that was uncommon on the mainland becomes common among their descendants. This best illustrates
o: the founder effect
Correct: A new population established by a few individuals carries only a sample of the source gene pool, so allele frequencies shift by chance.
gene flow
Gene flow requires ongoing migration between populations, not a one-time colonization.
directional selection
Directional selection requires a fitness difference favoring the allele, which is not described.
the bottleneck effect
A bottleneck is a drastic reduction of an existing population, not colonization of a new site.
questions.x: A new population established by a few individuals carries only a sample of the source gene pool, so allele frequencies shift by chance. Trap: Confusing founder effect (colonization) with bottleneck (population crash).

questions.q: Two genes are 50 cM apart on the same chromosome. How are their alleles expected to assort?
o: As if they were completely linked
Complete linkage would mean 0 percent recombination.
As if they were unlinked
Correct: A recombination frequency of 50 percent is the maximum and matches independent assortment, so the genes assort as if unlinked.
With 100 percent recombination
100 percent recombination is impossible because multiple crossovers cancel, capping frequency at 50 percent.
With no crossovers between them
No crossovers between them would also mean complete linkage.
questions.x: A recombination frequency of 50 percent is the maximum and matches independent assortment, so the genes assort as if unlinked. Trap: Thinking tightly linked genes cannot be 50 cM apart or that recombination can exceed 50 percent.

questions.q: A person carries a dominant disease allele but shows no signs of the disease, while a sibling with the same allele is severely affected. The first person's lack of phenotype is an example of
o: variable expressivity
Variable expressivity concerns differing severity among individuals who all show the trait, which does not describe a person with no signs.
codominance
Codominance describes two alleles both expressed in a heterozygote, not a missing phenotype.
epistasis
Epistasis describes one gene masking another, which is not given here.
incomplete penetrance
Correct: Penetrance is the fraction of individuals with a genotype who show any phenotype; carrying the allele with no signs reflects incomplete (reduced) penetrance.
questions.x: Penetrance is the fraction of individuals with a genotype who show any phenotype; carrying the allele with no signs reflects incomplete (reduced) penetrance. Trap: Mixing up penetrance (whether) and expressivity (how much).

questions.q: A father has a disease caused by a mutation in mitochondrial DNA. What proportion of his children is expected to inherit the mutation?
o: None of them
Correct: Mitochondria are inherited essentially from the egg cytoplasm, so mitochondrial mutations pass only through the mother and a father transmits none.
All of his sons
All his sons would inherit it only with paternal transmission, but sperm mitochondria do not contribute.
All of his daughters
All his daughters would inherit it only with paternal transmission, but sperm mitochondria do not contribute.
Half of his children
Half of his children would inherit it only with Mendelian paternal transmission, which does not apply to mtDNA.
questions.x: Mitochondria are inherited essentially from the egg cytoplasm, so mitochondrial mutations pass only through the mother and a father transmits none. Trap: Treating mitochondrial inheritance as sex-linked through the father.

questions.q: Loss of functional p53 in a cell with DNA damage would most likely result in
o: progression through the G1/S checkpoint with damaged DNA
Correct: p53 normally halts the cycle (via p21) or triggers apoptosis after damage; without it, damaged cells pass the G1/S checkpoint and keep dividing.
arrest in G2 with no possibility of progression
Loss of p53 removes arrest, so cells would not stay permanently arrested in G2.
accelerated apoptosis
Apoptosis would be reduced, not accelerated, without p53.
lengthening of telomeres
Telomere lengthening requires telomerase and is not directly caused by p53 loss.
questions.x: p53 normally halts the cycle (via p21) or triggers apoptosis after damage; without it, damaged cells pass the G1/S checkpoint and keep dividing. Trap: Thinking p53 promotes proliferation, as an oncogene would.

questions.q: An Hfr bacterium conjugates with an F- cell. What is the usual result?
o: The recipient becomes F+
The recipient does not become F+ because the F factor rarely reaches it.
The recipient becomes Hfr
The recipient does not become Hfr because the integrated F factor is not transferred.
The donor loses its entire chromosome
The donor retains its chromosome, since only a copy is transferred.
The recipient remains F- but may receive part of the donor chromosome

Correct: In Hfr cells the F factor is integrated in the chromosome and transferred last, so mating is usually interrupted before it enters and the recipient stays F- with part of the donor chromosome.
questions.x: In Hfr cells the F factor is integrated in the chromosome and transferred last, so mating is usually interrupted before it enters and the recipient stays F- with part of the donor chromosome. Trap: Treating Hfr like an F+ cell that transfers the F plasmid.

questions.q: A mule (horse 2n = 64, donkey 2n = 62) is usually sterile. What is the best explanation?
o: Its 63 chromosomes cannot pair normally during meiosis
Correct: Horse and donkey chromosomes differ in number and structure, so the mule's 63 chromosomes cannot synapse properly in meiosis and viable gametes rarely form.
It lacks an X chromosome
Mules have both sex chromosomes and are not lacking an X.
It is triploid
Mules are diploid hybrids, not triploid.
Its mitochondria cannot divide
Mitochondrial division is not the cause of sterility.
questions.x: Horse and donkey chromosomes differ in number and structure, so the mule's 63 chromosomes cannot synapse properly in meiosis and viable gametes rarely form. Trap: Believing sterility means the hybrid lacks a sex chromosome or is triploid rather than failing to pair homologs in meiosis.

questions.q: Ouabain inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase. How would the intestinal Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) be affected?
o: Reduced, because the Na+ gradient dissipates
Correct: SGLT relies on the Na+ gradient set up by the Na+/K+ ATPase; without the pump the gradient dissipates and glucose uptake falls.
Increased, because more Na+ is available
More Na+ is not available for cotransport, since the gradient collapses and uptake falls.
Unchanged, because SGLT uses ATP directly
SGLT is secondary active transport that uses the Na+ gradient, not ATP directly.
Reversed, because glucose moves down its gradient
SGLT does not reverse; the loss of the gradient reduces uptake rather than reversing flow.
questions.x: SGLT relies on the Na+ gradient set up by the Na+/K+ ATPase; without the pump the gradient dissipates and glucose uptake falls. Trap: Thinking cotransporters use ATP directly.

questions.q: A secreted protein follows which route?
o: Rough ER, Golgi, secretory vesicle, plasma membrane
Correct: Synthesis on the rough ER is followed by Golgi processing, packaging into secretory vesicles, and exocytosis at the plasma membrane.
Golgi, rough ER, lysosome, plasma membrane
Golgi before rough ER reverses the order, and lysosomes are not on the secretory route.
Nucleus, smooth ER, Golgi, lysosome
A secreted protein is not made in the nucleus, and the route ends in lysosomes rather than at the plasma membrane.
Smooth ER, Golgi, peroxisome
The smooth ER does not synthesize secreted proteins, and peroxisomes are not on the secretory route.
questions.x: Synthesis on the rough ER is followed by Golgi processing, packaging into secretory vesicles, and exocytosis at the plasma membrane. Trap: Placing the Golgi before the rough ER or routing a secreted protein through lysosomes or peroxisomes.

questions.q: Which epithelium is best suited for rapid gas exchange in the alveoli?
o: Stratified squamous epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium is thick and protective, like skin, which slows diffusion.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines airways to move mucus and is too thick for exchange.
Simple squamous epithelium
Correct: A thin single layer of flat cells minimizes diffusion distance, so simple squamous epithelium suits rapid gas exchange.
Simple columnar epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium is taller and suited to absorption and secretion, so diffusion distance is greater.
questions.x: A thin single layer of flat cells minimizes diffusion distance, so simple squamous epithelium suits rapid gas exchange. Trap: Choosing the protective epithelium of the skin.

questions.q: Multiple sclerosis involves immune-mediated loss of myelin in the CNS. Which consequence is expected?
o: Faster conduction because ion channels are exposed
Exposed channels along the axon do not speed conduction; current leaks and the signal weakens.
Loss of the all-or-none property of action potentials
The all-or-none property persists wherever an action potential is generated.
Slowed or blocked conduction because saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier is impaired
Correct: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, enabling fast saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier; demyelination slows or blocks propagation.
Increase in membrane capacitance that improves conduction
Demyelination increases capacitance, which worsens rather than improves conduction.
questions.x: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, enabling fast saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier; demyelination slows or blocks propagation. Trap: Thinking myelin loss helps because more channels are exposed.

questions.q: The absolute refractory period ensures that an action potential:
o: can fire again immediately with a larger stimulus
No stimulus, however large, can trigger another spike during the absolute refractory period.
is smaller if the stimulus is weak
Action potentials are all-or-none and do not scale with stimulus strength.
travels equally in both directions along the axon
The refractory region behind the impulse prevents backward travel, so propagation is unidirectional.
propagates in one direction because inactivated Na+ channels behind the impulse cannot reopen
Correct: Na+ channels behind the impulse are inactivated and cannot reopen, so the action potential propagates in one direction.
questions.x: Na+ channels behind the impulse are inactivated and cannot reopen, so the action potential propagates in one direction. Trap: Believing a stronger stimulus can overcome the absolute refractory period.

questions.q: A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m track in 80 s. What is her average velocity for the lap?
o: 0 m/s
Correct: Average velocity is displacement over time, and after one full lap she is back at the start, so displacement and average velocity are zero.
5 m/s
5 m/s is the average speed (400 m / 80 s), which uses distance rather than displacement.
10 m/s
10 m/s results from dividing 400 by 40 s or doubling the speed, with no physical basis.
400 m/s equals the distance itself and ignores dividing by time.
questions.x: Average velocity is displacement over time, and after one full lap she is back at the start, so displacement and average velocity are zero. Trap: Using distance rather than displacement.

questions.q: Use g = 10 m/s^2 where needed. A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed after 2.0 s?
o: 10 m/s
10 m/s is only the horizontal component and ignores vertical gain.
20 m/s
20 m/s is only the vertical component and ignores the horizontal.
22 m/s
Correct: Horizontal speed stays 10 m/s while vertical speed is gt = 20 m/s, so speed = sqrt(10^2 + 20^2) = sqrt(500), about 22 m/s.
30 m/s
30 m/s adds the perpendicular components arithmetically instead of vectorially.
questions.x: Horizontal speed stays 10 m/s while vertical speed is gt = 20 m/s, so speed = sqrt(10^2 + 20^2) = sqrt(500), about 22 m/s. Trap: Adding perpendicular velocity components arithmetically.

questions.q: A moving billiard ball strikes an identical stationary ball head-on in an elastic collision. After the collision:
o: both balls move at half the original velocity
Both moving at half speed conserves momentum but loses kinetic energy, so it is not elastic.
the first ball stops and the second moves with the original velocity
Correct: With equal masses, an elastic head-on collision conserves momentum and kinetic energy, so velocities are exchanged: the first ball stops and the second moves off at the original speed.
the balls stick together
Sticking together is a perfectly inelastic collision.
the first ball rebounds and the second moves with the same speed
The first ball rebounding with the second at the same speed would violate momentum conservation.
questions.x: With equal masses, an elastic head-on collision conserves momentum and kinetic energy, so velocities are exchanged: the first ball stops and the second moves off at the original speed. Trap: Applying the inelastic collision result.

questions.q: Use g = 10 m/s^2 where needed. A movable pulley is used to lift an 80 N load 2 m (ideal, no friction). Which values are correct?
o: 80 N force and 2 m of rope
80 N and 2 m is no machine at all and ignores the pulley advantage.
40 N force and 2 m of rope
40 N with only 2 m of rope would reduce work, which no ideal machine can do.
40 N force and 4 m of rope pulled
Correct: A movable pulley halves the force (40 N) while doubling the rope pulled (4 m), so work stays 160 J.
160 N force and 1 m of rope
160 N and 1 m reverses the force and distance trade.
questions.x: A movable pulley halves the force (40 N) while doubling the rope pulled (4 m), so work stays 160 J. Trap: Thinking machines reduce work.

questions.q: Two balls are launched on level ground at the same speed, one at 30 degrees and one at 60 degrees. Ignoring air resistance, which statement is correct?
o: The 30 degree ball has a greater range
The 30 degree ball does not outrange the 60 degree ball since ranges are equal.
They have equal ranges, and the 60 degree ball reaches a greater height
Correct: Range is proportional to sin(2 theta), equal for complementary angles 30 and 60, while height scales with sin^2(theta), so the 60 degree ball rises higher.
The 60 degree ball has a greater range and equal heights
The ranges are equal, not greater for 60 degrees, and heights differ.
They have equal ranges and equal heights
Ranges are equal but heights are not equal, since height depends on sin^2.
questions.x: Range is proportional to sin(2 theta), equal for complementary angles 30 and 60, while height scales with sin^2(theta), so the 60 degree ball rises higher. Trap: Thinking the largest angle gives the largest range.

questions.q: Use g = 10 m/s^2 where needed. A car travels around a flat circular curve of radius 20 m. If the coefficient of static friction is 0.5, what is the maximum speed without slipping?
o: 5 m/s
5 m/s does not follow from the equation and underestimates the speed.
100 m/s is v^2; the square root was not taken.
10 m/s
Correct: Friction supplies centripetal force: mu m g = m v^2/r, so v = sqrt(mu g r) = sqrt(0.5 x 10 x 20) = 10 m/s.
14 m/s
14 m/s is sqrt(200), from dropping the 0.5 factor.
questions.x: Friction supplies centripetal force: mu m g = m v^2/r, so v = sqrt(mu g r) = sqrt(0.5 x 10 x 20) = 10 m/s. Trap: Forgetting to take the square root.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. The net work done on the satellite by gravity in one orbit is:
o: positive, because gravity accelerates the satellite
Gravity does not do positive work here; speed is constant.
negative, because gravity opposes outward motion
The satellite does not move outward or inward in a circular orbit, so there is no negative work.
equal to the kinetic energy of the satellite
Net work equals the change in kinetic energy, which is zero, not equal to the kinetic energy.
zero, because the force is perpendicular to the displacement at all times
Correct: Gravity acts toward the center, perpendicular to velocity, so W = Fd cos 90 = 0 and kinetic energy stays constant.
questions.x: Gravity acts toward the center, perpendicular to velocity, so W = Fd cos 90 = 0 and kinetic energy stays constant. Trap: Thinking any force that causes acceleration does work.

questions.q: Why does bending the knees when landing from a jump reduce the risk of injury?
o: It reduces the change in momentum of the body
The momentum change is fixed by landing speed and mass, and bending the knees does not reduce it.
It increases the average force over a shorter time
Bending knees increases the stopping time, not shortens it, so force goes down, not up.
It lengthens the stopping time, reducing the average force for the same change in momentum
Correct: Impulse F_avg = delta p / delta t, so lengthening the stopping time reduces the average force for the same momentum change.
It reduces the person's mass
Mass does not change when bending the knees.
questions.x: Impulse F_avg = delta p / delta t, so lengthening the stopping time reduces the average force for the same momentum change. Trap: Believing momentum changes by a different amount.

questions.q: Blood flows from the aorta into the capillary beds, whose total cross-sectional area is roughly 1000 times that of the aorta. Compared with aortic flow, the blood velocity in the capillaries is:
o: much higher, because capillary radius is so small
each capillary is narrow, but velocity depends on the summed area of all parallel capillaries, which is huge, so velocity is lower, not higher.
unchanged, because pressure is constant across the circuit
pressure falls steadily along the circuit and is not constant; velocity is set by continuity, not by constant pressure.
higher, because capillary resistance is greatest
high resistance lowers the pressure, but velocity is governed by total cross-sectional area, not by resistance.
much lower, because total cross-sectional area is greatest there
Correct: Continuity (A1v1 = A2v2) means velocity falls as total cross-sectional area rises, which is why capillary flow is slow enough for exchange.
questions.x: Continuity (A1v1 = A2v2) means velocity falls as total cross-sectional area rises, which is why capillary flow is slow enough for exchange. Trap: Looking at a single capillary's tiny radius instead of the total cross-sectional area of all capillaries in parallel.

questions.q: A horizontal artery has a localized atherosclerotic narrowing. In the narrowed segment, compared with the normal segment, the blood has:
o: higher velocity and lower pressure
Correct: Continuity requires faster flow in the narrow segment, and Bernoulli's principle then requires lower static pressure at the same height.
higher velocity and higher pressure
faster flow cannot coincide with higher pressure in a horizontal ideal fluid; Bernoulli trades pressure for kinetic energy.
lower velocity and higher pressure
velocity cannot fall in a constriction, since the same flow must pass through a smaller area.
lower velocity and lower pressure
velocity would rise, not fall, in the narrowing, so slower flow contradicts continuity.
questions.x: Continuity requires faster flow in the narrow segment, and Bernoulli's principle then requires lower static pressure at the same height. Trap: Assuming the narrowed region has higher pressure because it is 'squeezed'.

questions.q: Compared with hemoglobin, myoglobin in muscle has:
o: a hyperbolic curve and higher affinity at low PO2
Correct: Myoglobin is a monomer with no cooperativity and a left-shifted hyperbolic curve, so it takes oxygen from hemoglobin and stores it.
a sigmoidal curve and lower affinity at low PO2
a sigmoidal curve requires multiple cooperative subunits, and lower affinity would stop oxygen transfer from blood to muscle.
a sigmoidal curve and higher affinity
myoglobin has a single subunit so it cannot be sigmoidal, even though its affinity is higher.
a hyperbolic curve and lower affinity at low PO2
the hyperbolic shape is right, but lower affinity would prevent myoglobin from taking oxygen from hemoglobin.
questions.x: Myoglobin is a monomer with no cooperativity and a left-shifted hyperbolic curve, so it takes oxygen from hemoglobin and stores it. Trap: Assigning cooperativity to a single-subunit protein.

questions.q: A patient with polycythemia has a markedly elevated hematocrit. If the pressure gradient across a vessel is unchanged, the flow rate through the vessel will:
o: increase, because oxygen content rises
extra oxygen-carrying capacity does not change the fluid mechanics, and flow actually falls.
remain unchanged, because radius is unchanged
radius is not the only determinant of resistance; viscosity also enters directly.
decrease, because viscosity and resistance rise
Correct: Poiseuille's law makes resistance proportional to viscosity, so higher hematocrit increases resistance and lowers Q for a fixed pressure gradient.
increase, because density rises
density is not in Poiseuille's law, and the viscosity increase reduces flow.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law makes resistance proportional to viscosity, so higher hematocrit increases resistance and lowers Q for a fixed pressure gradient. Trap: Assuming only vessel radius influences resistance.

questions.q: The lymphatic system helps maintain fluid balance primarily by:
o: actively transporting oxygen to tissues
lymphatics do not transport oxygen; that is the job of blood and hemoglobin.
increasing capillary oncotic pressure directly
lymph does not directly raise capillary oncotic pressure; returning protein only indirectly maintains the gradient.
returning excess filtered interstitial fluid and protein to the venous circulation
Correct: Net filtration at capillaries exceeds reabsorption, and lymph returns the surplus interstitial fluid and protein to the veins.
absorbing water from arterioles
lymphatics collect fluid from the interstitium, not from arterioles.
questions.x: Net filtration at capillaries exceeds reabsorption, and lymph returns the surplus interstitial fluid and protein to the veins. Trap: Overlooking that capillaries filter more than they reabsorb.

questions.q: Without surfactant, small alveoli tend to collapse and empty into larger alveoli because:
o: pressure from surface tension is inversely proportional to radius
Correct: Laplace's law for a sphere gives P = 2T/r, so smaller radius means higher pressure, and small alveoli empty into larger ones unless surfactant lowers T.
wall tension is proportional to radius
wall tension is not the cause; in the alveolar form pressure is inversely, not directly, related to radius.
small alveoli have greater compliance
small alveoli have lower, not greater, compliance because of their higher collapsing pressure.
large alveoli have higher surface tension
large alveoli do not have higher surface tension; the problem is pressure being highest in the small ones.
questions.x: Laplace's law for a sphere gives P = 2T/r, so smaller radius means higher pressure, and small alveoli empty into larger ones unless surfactant lowers T. Trap: Applying the vessel wall-tension form (T = Pr) to alveoli.

questions.q: During inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm causes air to enter the lungs because:
o: thoracic volume decreases and pressure rises
thoracic volume increases, not decreases, and rising pressure would push air out.
thoracic volume increases and intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric
Correct: Diaphragm contraction increases thoracic volume; by Boyle's law (PV constant) pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in down the gradient.
alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric
alveolar pressure above atmospheric would drive expiration, not inspiration.
lung tissue actively pulls in air
lung tissue is passive and follows the chest wall; it does not actively pull air in.
questions.x: Diaphragm contraction increases thoracic volume; by Boyle's law (PV constant) pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in down the gradient. Trap: Believing inspiration is pushing air in rather than a pressure gradient created by volume change.

questions.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has thickened alveolar walls. According to Fick's law, the rate of gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane will:
o: increase, because surface area increases
fibrosis does not increase surface area, and if anything area is lost.
remain unchanged, because partial pressures are unchanged
thickness is part of the rate expression, so unchanged partial pressures do not keep the rate unchanged.
increase, because tissue density increases
tissue density is not a term in Fick's law, and denser tissue would not speed diffusion.
decrease, because diffusion distance increases
Correct: Fick's law makes diffusion rate proportional to area x pressure difference / thickness, so thickened walls lower the rate.
questions.x: Fick's law makes diffusion rate proportional to area x pressure difference / thickness, so thickened walls lower the rate. Trap: Forgetting thickness is in the denominator of Fick's law.

questions.q: Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds more CO2 and H+ than oxygenated hemoglobin. This helps in systemic tissues because:
o: oxygen release promotes uptake of CO2 as blood leaves the tissues
Correct: The Haldane effect: lower oxygen saturation increases hemoglobin's CO2 and H+ binding, aiding CO2 pickup as oxygen is released in tissues.
oxygen release causes CO2 release
oxygen release promotes CO2 binding, not release; CO2 release happens in the lungs.
it shifts the curve left
a left shift would raise affinity and impair unloading, and it is not the Haldane effect.
CO2 uptake prevents oxygen unloading
CO2 uptake and H+ binding promote (Bohr effect) rather than prevent oxygen unloading.
questions.x: The Haldane effect: lower oxygen saturation increases hemoglobin's CO2 and H+ binding, aiding CO2 pickup as oxygen is released in tissues. Trap: Confusing the Haldane effect with the Bohr effect.

questions.q: CO2 diffuses readily from pulmonary capillary blood into alveoli even though its partial pressure gradient is only about 6 mmHg, because CO2:
o: has a higher molecular mass than O2
higher molecular mass would slow, not speed, diffusion, and solubility is the dominant factor.
is much more soluble in the membrane and plasma than O2
Correct: Diffusion rate depends on the gradient and on solubility in the membrane and plasma; CO2 is about 20 times more soluble than O2, offsetting its small gradient.
is bound to hemoglobin with greater affinity
hemoglobin binding does not drive diffusion across the alveolar membrane; CO2 largely travels as bicarbonate.
is actively transported
CO2 crosses the membrane passively by diffusion; no active transport is involved.
questions.x: Diffusion rate depends on the gradient and on solubility in the membrane and plasma; CO2 is about 20 times more soluble than O2, offsetting its small gradient. Trap: Assuming a small gradient implies a slow diffusion.

questions.q: Veins hold most of the blood volume and return it to the heart at low pressure. Which feature most directly prevents backflow in the legs?
o: thick muscular walls
veins have thin, not thick muscular, walls; that describes arteries.
one-way valves assisted by skeletal muscle contraction
Correct: One-way venous valves plus the skeletal muscle pump push blood toward the heart and prevent backflow in the legs.
high hydrostatic pressure
high hydrostatic pressure in the legs favors pooling rather than preventing backflow.
pulsatile flow from capillaries
capillary outflow is not pulsatile, since pulsation is damped by the arterial tree.
questions.x: One-way venous valves plus the skeletal muscle pump push blood toward the heart and prevent backflow in the legs. Trap: Assigning arterial properties to veins.

questions.q: Mixed venous blood entering a pulmonary capillary has a PO2 of about 40 mmHg, and alveolar PO2 is about 100 mmHg. Which statement describes oxygen movement?
o: oxygen diffuses passively from alveolar air into the capillary blood until the partial pressures nearly equalize
Correct: Gas exchange is passive and follows partial pressure gradients, so oxygen moves from alveolar air (100 mmHg) into blood (40 mmHg) until they nearly equalize.
oxygen is actively pumped into the blood against its gradient
oxygen is not actively pumped; diffusion alone suffices.
oxygen diffuses from the blood into the alveoli
the gradient favors movement into the blood, not out of it.
oxygen movement stops because hemoglobin is already saturated
hemoglobin at a PO2 of 40 mmHg is only about 75% saturated, so loading continues.
questions.x: Gas exchange is passive and follows partial pressure gradients, so oxygen moves from alveolar air (100 mmHg) into blood (40 mmHg) until they nearly equalize. Trap: Believing gas exchange needs active transport.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell, electrons flow through the external wire from:
o: the cathode, where oxidation occurs, to the anode
reverses the electrode roles; oxidation never occurs at the cathode and electrons do not flow cathode to anode.
the anode, where reduction occurs, to the cathode
reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode, so this mislabels the anode's process.
the cathode, where reduction occurs, to the anode
electrons flow from anode to cathode, so this reverses the direction even though reduction at the cathode is right.
the anode, where oxidation occurs, to the cathode, where reduction occurs
Correct: Oxidation at the anode releases electrons that travel through the external wire to the cathode, where they reduce a species.
questions.x: Oxidation at the anode releases electrons that travel through the external wire to the cathode, where they reduce a species. Trap: Mixing up the direction of electron flow with conventional current.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes an electrolytic cell?
o: It converts spontaneous reaction energy into current, with oxidation at the cathode
describes a galvanic cell, and oxidation never occurs at the cathode.
It has a positive E0cell and delta G less than zero
a positive E0cell with negative delta G describes a spontaneous galvanic cell.
It has reduction at the anode because the anode is negative
reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode, in every cell; only the electrode's sign changes.
It uses an external power source to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction, with reduction at the cathode
Correct: An electrolytic cell uses an external power source to drive a nonspontaneous reaction (delta G > 0, E0cell < 0), and reduction still occurs at the cathode.
questions.x: An electrolytic cell uses an external power source to drive a nonspontaneous reaction (delta G > 0, E0cell < 0), and reduction still occurs at the cathode. Trap: Assuming electrode roles flip in electrolytic cells.

questions.q: A redox reaction has a positive standard cell potential. Which must be true?
o: delta G0 is positive and K is greater than 1
a positive delta G0 would correspond to a negative E0, and K greater than 1 requires a negative delta G0.
delta G0 is negative and K is less than 1
delta G0 is negative but K is then greater than 1, not less.
delta G0 is positive and K is less than 1
a positive delta G0 and K less than 1 describe a nonspontaneous reaction with negative E0.
delta G0 is negative and K is greater than 1
Correct: delta G0 = -nFE0 = -RT ln K, so a positive E0 gives a negative delta G0 and K greater than 1.
questions.x: delta G0 = -nFE0 = -RT ln K, so a positive E0 gives a negative delta G0 and K greater than 1. Trap: Mixing the signs of delta G0 and ln K.

questions.q: During recharging of a lead-acid or lithium-ion battery, the cell functions as:
o: an electrolytic cell, driving the reverse of the discharge reaction
Correct: Recharging uses an external source to force the nonspontaneous reverse reaction, so the cell acts as an electrolytic cell.
a galvanic cell with reversed electrodes
a galvanic cell produces current spontaneously and cannot be recharged by simply reversing electrodes.
a concentration cell
a concentration cell runs on a concentration gradient, not on the discharge chemistry reversal.
a fuel cell
a fuel cell is continuously supplied with reactants and is not a recharged battery.
questions.x: Recharging uses an external source to force the nonspontaneous reverse reaction, so the cell acts as an electrolytic cell. Trap: Assuming that the cell stays galvanic during charging.

questions.q: In a concentration cell with Cu electrodes in 0.1 M and 1.0 M Cu2+ solutions, electrons flow externally from:
o: the 1.0 M half-cell to the 0.1 M half-cell
this reverses the direction; the concentrated cell is the cathode where Cu2+ is reduced.
the 0.1 M half-cell to the 1.0 M half-cell
Correct: The dilute half-cell is the anode, where Cu oxidizes to raise its concentration, so electrons flow from 0.1 M to 1.0 M.
neither, because E0 = 0
E0 is zero, but E = -(0.06/n) log Q is nonzero when concentrations differ, so current flows.
the cathode to the anode
electrons do flow anode to cathode, so cathode to anode is backward.
questions.x: The dilute half-cell is the anode, where Cu oxidizes to raise its concentration, so electrons flow from 0.1 M to 1.0 M. Trap: Concluding no current because E0 = 0.

questions.q: When the half-reaction Ag+ + e- -> Ag (E0 = +0.80 V) is multiplied by 2 to balance electrons in a full reaction, the E0 for the half-reaction becomes:
o: +1.60 V scales E0 by 2, as if it were extensive.
+0.40 V halves E0, which is likewise not how potentials behave.
-0.80 V flips the sign, which applies only to reversing the half-reaction.
Correct: Reduction potential is intensive and does not scale with stoichiometric coefficients, so E0 stays +0.80 V.
questions.x: Reduction potential is intensive and does not scale with stoichiometric coefficients, so E0 stays +0.80 V. Trap: Scaling E0 with stoichiometric coefficients as if it were an extensive quantity like delta G.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of molten NaCl, the products at the cathode and anode are, respectively:
o: Na(l) and Cl2(g)
Correct: In molten NaCl, Na+ is reduced to Na(l) at the cathode and Cl- is oxidized to Cl2(g) at the anode.
Cl2(g) and Na(l)
reverses the electrode roles; sodium cations cannot be oxidized to Na and chloride is not reduced to Cl2.
H2(g) and Cl2(g)
H2 requires water, which is absent in the molten salt, and the Cl2 half is the only correct piece.
Na(l) and O2(g)
O2 would require water; no oxygen source exists in molten NaCl, and chloride is oxidized instead.
questions.x: In molten NaCl, Na+ is reduced to Na(l) at the cathode and Cl- is oxidized to Cl2(g) at the anode. Trap: Applying aqueous electrolysis products to a molten salt.

questions.q: A dielectric is inserted into a charged capacitor that has been disconnected from the battery. Which change occurs?
o: the voltage across the capacitor increases
an increase in V would require a decrease in C, but the dielectric raises C.
the charge on the plates increases
charge cannot increase on an isolated capacitor since there is no source.
the voltage across the capacitor decreases
Correct: With the battery disconnected, Q is fixed; the dielectric raises C by kappa, so V = Q/C falls.
the charge on the plates decreases
charge cannot leave an isolated capacitor, so it stays constant.
questions.x: With the battery disconnected, Q is fixed; the dielectric raises C by kappa, so V = Q/C falls. Trap: Assuming charge changes when the capacitor is isolated.

questions.q: To measure the voltage across a resistor and the current through it, a voltmeter and ammeter should be connected, respectively:
o: in series with the resistor and in parallel with the resistor
this reverses the placements and would short out the circuit through the ammeter.
both in series
a voltmeter in series would block current and read no potential difference across the resistor.
both in parallel
an ammeter in parallel is nearly a short circuit and would not measure the resistor's current.
in parallel with the resistor and in series with the resistor
Correct: A voltmeter reads a potential difference, so it goes in parallel (high resistance); an ammeter measures current, so it goes in series (low resistance).
questions.x: A voltmeter reads a potential difference, so it goes in parallel (high resistance); an ammeter measures current, so it goes in series (low resistance). Trap: Reversing meter placements, putting the voltmeter in series and the ammeter in parallel.

questions.q: In a metal wire connected to a battery, conventional current flows:
o: from the positive terminal toward the negative terminal, opposite to electron flow
Correct: Conventional current is defined as the flow of positive charge, from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to electron motion.
from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal
this describes the direction electrons move, not conventional current.
in the same direction as electron flow
conventional current is opposite to electron flow, not the same.
in alternating directions
a battery provides DC, which has a constant direction.
questions.x: Conventional current is defined as the flow of positive charge, from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to electron motion. Trap: Equating conventional current with electron flow.

questions.q: Myelination speeds nerve conduction mainly because it:
o: decreases membrane resistance
lower resistance would increase leakage and slow conduction.
increases membrane capacitance
higher capacitance would slow charging of the membrane.
adds more ion channels along the sheath
ion channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier, not along the sheath.
increases membrane resistance and decreases membrane capacitance
Correct: Myelin acts as extra insulation, raising membrane resistance and lowering capacitance, so less current leaks and less charge is needed to depolarize the next node.
questions.x: Myelin acts as extra insulation, raising membrane resistance and lowering capacitance, so less current leaks and less charge is needed to depolarize the next node. Trap: Assuming that myelin adds capacitance.

questions.q: A 4 ohm resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 6 ohm and 3 ohm resistors, all powered by a 12 V battery. The current through the 6 ohm resistor is approximately:
o: Correct: The parallel pair is 2 ohms, so the total is 6 ohms and I = 2 A; the parallel voltage is 12 - 2 x 4 = 4 V, so I(6 ohm) = 4/6 = 0.67 A.
0.33 A has no basis in this circuit and is an arithmetic slip.
1.33 A is the current through the 3 ohm branch (4/3).
2.0 A is the total current, not the branch current.
questions.x: The parallel pair is 2 ohms, so the total is 6 ohms and I = 2 A; the parallel voltage is 12 - 2 x 4 = 4 V, so I(6 ohm) = 4/6 = 0.67 A. Trap: Giving total current rather than branch current.

questions.q: The mass of a stable nucleus is slightly less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons because:
o: neutrons convert into protons
neutron-to-proton conversion is beta decay and does not explain the mass deficit.
some nucleons are destroyed
nucleons are conserved; none are destroyed.
energy is released on formation, corresponding to binding energy via E = mc^2
Correct: The mass defect is the mass equivalent (E = mc^2) of the binding energy released when the nucleus formed, so the nucleus weighs less than its separated nucleons.
electrons shield the nucleus
electron shielding is an atomic effect and irrelevant to nuclear mass.
questions.x: The mass defect is the mass equivalent (E = mc^2) of the binding energy released when the nucleus formed, so the nucleus weighs less than its separated nucleons. Trap: Thinking the mass defect means that nucleons vanish.

questions.q: A hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2, then another falls from n = 2 to n = 1. The photon from the n = 2 to n = 1 transition has:
o: greater energy and shorter wavelength
Correct: Energy gaps between levels shrink with increasing n, so the 2-to-1 gap is larger than 3-to-2, giving a more energetic photon with a shorter wavelength (E = hc/lambda).
less energy and longer wavelength
less energy would mean a longer wavelength, but the 2-to-1 gap is the larger one.
greater energy and longer wavelength
greater energy corresponds to a shorter wavelength, not a longer one.
the same energy
different transitions emit different photon energies.
questions.x: Energy gaps between levels shrink with increasing n, so the 2-to-1 gap is larger than 3-to-2, giving a more energetic photon with a shorter wavelength (E = hc/lambda). Trap: Assuming all transitions to a lower level emit equal energy.

questions.q: Which element has the highest first ionization energy?
o: neon
Correct: Ionization energy rises across a period, and noble gases with filled shells have the highest values, so neon is the highest here.
sodium
sodium is an alkali metal with one loosely held valence electron and low IE.
magnesium
magnesium is a metal with a low IE compared with the nonmetals.
fluorine
fluorine has a high IE but a lower one than neon, which is a filled shell.
questions.x: Ionization energy rises across a period, and noble gases with filled shells have the highest values, so neon is the highest here. Trap: Picking fluorine as the extreme due to electronegativity.

questions.q: Which element is expected to have the most exothermic electron affinity?
o: neon
neon has a filled shell and an electron affinity near zero or endothermic.
sodium
sodium is an alkali metal that gains an electron only weakly.
magnesium
magnesium has a filled 3s subshell, so adding an electron is near zero or endothermic.
chlorine
Correct: Halogens strongly attract an added electron to complete the octet, and chlorine has the most exothermic electron affinity (slightly more than fluorine, whose small size causes repulsion).
questions.x: Halogens strongly attract an added electron to complete the octet, and chlorine has the most exothermic electron affinity (slightly more than fluorine, whose small size causes repulsion). Trap: Assuming fluorine must be the highest in EA.

questions.q: The ground-state electron configuration of nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3) shows the three 2p electrons:
o: occupying separate orbitals with parallel spins
Correct: Hund's rule fills degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing, so the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins.
paired in one orbital with one empty orbital
pairing two electrons in one 2p orbital while another is empty violates Hund's rule.
occupying separate orbitals with antiparallel spins
antiparallel spins in separate orbitals would lower the exchange stabilization that Hund's rule favors.
paired in two orbitals
three electrons cannot be paired in two orbitals without leaving one unpaired.
questions.x: Hund's rule fills degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing, so the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins. Trap: Pairing electrons before filling every orbital.

questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency (frequency fixed) will:
o: increase the maximum kinetic energy of each electron
intensity does not change photon energy, so KEmax is unchanged.
increase the number of photoelectrons but not their maximum kinetic energy
Correct: KEmax = hf - phi depends on the frequency, while intensity changes only the number of photons, so more electrons are ejected with the same maximum kinetic energy.
decrease the number of ejected electrons
more photons eject more electrons, not fewer.
change the threshold frequency
the threshold frequency depends on the work function of the metal, not on intensity.
questions.x: KEmax = hf - phi depends on the frequency, while intensity changes only the number of photons, so more electrons are ejected with the same maximum kinetic energy. Trap: Using classical wave theory, where intensity raises KE.

questions.q: Transition metals often form colored compounds with multiple oxidation states because:
o: they have full outer s subshells only
full outer s subshells alone would not give color or variable oxidation states.
they have very high electronegativities
transition metals have low to moderate electronegativity, and electronegativity does not cause color.
they lack valence electrons
transition metals have valence electrons in ns and (n-1)d, so they do not lack them.
their partially filled d orbitals allow close-lying energy levels and d-d transitions
Correct: Partially filled d orbitals have close-lying energy levels, allowing d-d transitions (color) and similar ns and (n-1)d energies (multiple oxidation states).
questions.x: Partially filled d orbitals have close-lying energy levels, allowing d-d transitions (color) and similar ns and (n-1)d energies (multiple oxidation states). Trap: Attributing color to electronegativity.

questions.q: Moving from sodium to chlorine across period 3, the effective nuclear charge experienced by valence electrons:
o: decreases, because more electrons are added
added electrons go into the same shell and shield poorly, so Zeff does not decrease.
increases, because shielding by inner electrons stays about the same while Z increases
Correct: Across period 3, protons are added while same-shell electrons shield poorly and inner shielding stays about the same, so Zeff increases and the radius shrinks.
stays constant
Zeff rises as protons are added.
increases, because more shells are added
no new shell is added across a period.
questions.x: Across period 3, protons are added while same-shell electrons shield poorly and inner shielding stays about the same, so Zeff increases and the radius shrinks. Trap: Thinking added electrons increase shielding in the same shell.

questions.q: An element has the following successive ionization energies in kJ/mol: 577, 1817, 2745, 11,577. The element most likely has how many valence electrons?
o: 2 would put the jump after the second value;
4 would put it after the fourth;
Correct: The large jump after the third ionization energy (2745 to 11,577) means the fourth electron comes from an inner shell, so there are three valence electrons.
1 would put it after the first. The jump position, not the size of the first value, gives the valence count.
questions.x: The large jump after the third ionization energy (2745 to 11,577) means the fourth electron comes from an inner shell, so there are three valence electrons. Trap: Reading the jump position incorrectly.

questions.q: Which ranking of typical interaction strengths is correct, strongest to weakest?
o: London dispersion > hydrogen bond > ion-dipole > dipole-dipole
Places dispersion first and ion-dipole and dipole-dipole in reverse order.
Dipole-dipole > ion-dipole > London dispersion > hydrogen bond
Places dipole-dipole first and hydrogen bonds last, which scrambles the order.
Ion-dipole > hydrogen bond > dipole-dipole > London dispersion (for comparable small molecules)
Correct: Charge-involving interactions are strongest, followed by hydrogen bonds, then permanent dipoles, then transient induced dipoles.
Hydrogen bond > London dispersion > ion-dipole > dipole-dipole
Places hydrogen bond above ion-dipole and dispersion above dipole-dipole, both incorrect.
questions.x: Charge-involving interactions are strongest, followed by hydrogen bonds, then permanent dipoles, then transient induced dipoles. Trap: Forgetting that ion-dipole interactions outrank hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: A DNA duplex rich in G-C pairs has a higher melting temperature than an A-T-rich duplex because:
o: G-C pairs form covalent bonds
Says G-C pairs form covalent bonds, but base pairs are held by non-covalent hydrogen bonds.
G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds, A-T pairs only two
Correct: G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T, and stack more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate the strands.
A-T pairs contain more phosphate
Says A-T pairs contain more phosphate, but phosphates are in the backbone, not the pairing.
G is a pyrimidine and A is a purine
Says G is a pyrimidine and A a purine, but both are purines.
questions.x: G-C pairs share three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T, and stack more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate the strands. Trap: Confusing hydrogen bond count between G-C and A-T.

questions.q: Compressing ice at a temperature slightly below 0 C can cause it to melt. Which feature of the phase diagram explains this?
o: The solid-liquid boundary has a negative slope
Correct: Because ice is less dense than water, increased pressure favors the liquid, so the solid-liquid boundary slopes backward (negative slope).
The triple point lies at high pressure
The triple point location does not explain melting under compression.
The critical point is above 100 C
The critical point concerns liquid-gas behavior, not ice melting under pressure.
The sublimation curve is horizontal
Sublimation curves slope upward, not horizontally, and relate to solid-gas transition.
questions.x: Because ice is less dense than water, increased pressure favors the liquid, so the solid-liquid boundary slopes backward (negative slope). Trap: Assuming the solid-liquid line always slopes positively.

questions.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate toward the:
o: Cathode, with larger fragments moving faster
Cathode with larger fragments faster is wrong on both direction and size dependence.
Anode, with larger fragments moving faster
Anode with larger fragments faster is right on direction but reverses size dependence.
Anode (positive electrode), with smaller fragments moving faster
Correct: The phosphate backbone is negatively charged so DNA moves toward the anode, and smaller fragments pass through pores more easily.
Cathode, with smaller fragments moving faster
Cathode with smaller fragments faster is wrong on direction because negative DNA does not go to the negative electrode.
questions.x: The phosphate backbone is negatively charged so DNA moves toward the anode, and smaller fragments pass through pores more easily. Trap: Forgetting that DNA is negatively charged, so it moves to the positive electrode, or reversing which fragments move faster through the gel.

questions.q: Which compound mixture could be purified by sublimation?
o: Two liquids with similar boiling points
Two liquids of similar boiling points would need fractional distillation.
A solid that has a significant vapor pressure below its melting point mixed with nonvolatile impurities
Correct: A solid with significant vapor pressure below its melting point vaporizes and re-deposits on a cold surface, leaving nonvolatile impurities behind.
A salt dissolved in water
A salt dissolved in water is separated by evaporation or crystallization, not sublimation.
Two proteins of differing mass
Two proteins of differing mass are separated by chromatography or electrophoresis.
questions.x: A solid with significant vapor pressure below its melting point vaporizes and re-deposits on a cold surface, leaving nonvolatile impurities behind. Trap: Assuming sublimation only applies to dry ice.

questions.q: For a reaction at constant temperature, Q is less than K. Which is true?
o: ΔG is positive and the reaction proceeds in the forward direction
A positive ΔG would mean Q > K, so no forward drive.
ΔG is negative and the reaction proceeds in reverse
A negative ΔG means spontaneous forward direction, not reverse.
ΔG is negative and the reaction proceeds in the forward direction
Correct: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K); when Q < K the log is negative, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction proceeds forward, making products until Q = K.
ΔG is zero and the system is at equilibrium
ΔG = 0 only when Q = K, which is not the case here.
questions.x: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K); when Q < K the log is negative, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction proceeds forward, making products until Q = K. Trap: Reversing the Q/K comparison: Q < K means too many reactants, so forward shift.

questions.q: Which statement about bond energies is correct?
o: Breaking bonds requires energy input, and forming bonds releases energy
Correct: Bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic, so ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed).
Breaking bonds releases energy
Breaking bonds requires energy input; it never releases energy.
Forming bonds requires energy input
Forming bonds releases energy rather than requiring it.
Breaking and forming bonds are both exothermic
Breaking is endothermic, so the two processes cannot both be exothermic.
questions.x: Bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic, so ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed). Trap: Thinking energy is released when a bond 'breaks', as in ATP hydrolysis folklore.

questions.q: A mechanism has a slow first step A + B → C and a fast second step C + B → D. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[A][B]^2
Squaring [B] uses the overall stoichiometry (two B consumed) rather than the slow step.
rate = k[C][B]
C is an intermediate and its step is fast, so it cannot be in the rate law.
rate = k[D]
D is the final product and does not influence the rate.
rate = k[A][B]
Correct: The rate law follows the slow (rate-determining) step, whose reactants are A and B, each first order, so rate = k[A][B].
questions.x: The rate law follows the slow (rate-determining) step, whose reactants are A and B, each first order, so rate = k[A][B]. Trap: Using overall stoichiometry for the rate law rather than the slowest step.

questions.q: An exothermic reaction is carried out in an insulated calorimeter. What is observed?
o: The temperature of the surroundings decreases and ΔH is negative
Surroundings cooling would indicate an endothermic reaction, though ΔH negative is mismatched with it.
The temperature increases and ΔH is positive
A temperature rise is correct, but exothermic reactions have negative, not positive, ΔH.
The temperature of the surroundings increases and ΔH is negative
Correct: An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, raising their temperature, and ΔH < 0.
The temperature is unchanged because energy is conserved
Energy is conserved but is transferred as heat, so temperature changes.
questions.x: An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, raising their temperature, and ΔH < 0. Trap: Taking the system's perspective and assuming an exothermic reaction cools, when the surroundings absorb the released heat.

questions.q: On a reaction coordinate diagram, the transition state is:
o: the highest-energy point along the pathway, which cannot be isolated
Correct: The transition state is the energy maximum along the reaction coordinate, and it is too short-lived to isolate.
a local energy minimum between steps
A local energy minimum between steps is an intermediate, which can sometimes be isolated.
the energy of the products
The energy of the products is the final level on the diagram, not a peak.
the difference between reactants and products
The difference between reactants and products is ΔG (or ΔH), not a species on the pathway.
questions.x: The transition state is the energy maximum along the reaction coordinate, and it is too short-lived to isolate. Trap: Confusing transition states with reaction intermediates.

questions.q: A reaction with negative ΔH and negative ΔS is:
o: spontaneous at all temperatures
Spontaneity at all temperatures needs negative ΔH and positive ΔS.
spontaneous at high temperature only
High-temperature-only spontaneity needs positive ΔH and positive ΔS.
nonspontaneous at all temperatures
Nonspontaneity at all temperatures needs positive ΔH and negative ΔS.
spontaneous at low temperature only
Correct: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS; with both negative, the negative ΔH dominates at low T (ΔG < 0) but -TΔS turns positive at high T.
questions.x: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS; with both negative, the negative ΔH dominates at low T (ΔG < 0) but -TΔS turns positive at high T. Trap: Mixing up which sign combinations give temperature-dependent spontaneity.

questions.q: The absolute threshold is best defined as the:
o: minimum difference between two stimuli detected 50% of the time
This describes the difference threshold (just noticeable difference), which concerns two stimuli.
intensity at which a stimulus is detected 100% of the time
There is no intensity at which detection is a certain 100%, because of noise.
minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time
Correct: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time, since detection is probabilistic.
intensity at which a stimulus becomes painful
The point where a stimulus becomes painful is a pain threshold, not the absolute threshold.
questions.x: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time, since detection is probabilistic. Trap: Confusing absolute threshold with the difference threshold.

questions.q: After a few minutes in a room, you no longer notice a perfume odor. This is an example of:
o: habituation to a cognitive expectation
Habituation is a central decline in response to repeated stimuli and is not tied to a cognitive expectation here.
sensory adaptation
Correct: A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a constant stimulus is sensory adaptation.
absolute threshold elevation due to damage
No damage occurred; the odor is noticed again when the stimulus changes.
selective attention to the odor
Selective attention would be a shift of focus, not a fading of perception under constant stimulation.
questions.x: A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a constant stimulus is sensory adaptation. Trap: Confusing sensory adaptation (receptor-level) with habituation (central).

questions.q: In hearing, mechanical energy is converted to neural signals by:
o: hair cells in the organ of Corti bending against the tectorial membrane
Correct: Hair cells in the organ of Corti are bent against the tectorial membrane, opening ion channels and depolarizing them (transduction).
the ossicles vibrating the round window
The ossicles amplify mechanical vibration and push on the oval window, not the round window, without transducing.
photoreceptors in the cochlea
The cochlea contains hair cells, not photoreceptors.
the tympanic membrane generating action potentials
The eardrum vibrates mechanically and does not generate action potentials.
questions.x: Hair cells in the organ of Corti are bent against the tectorial membrane, opening ion channels and depolarizing them (transduction). Trap: Thinking the eardrum or ossicles perform transduction.

questions.q: Meditating to calm oneself after an unavoidable loss is:
o: problem-focused coping
Problem-focused coping would try to change the situation, which is impossible here.
emotion-focused coping
Correct: Meditation after an unavoidable loss manages emotional distress rather than changing the situation, which is emotion-focused coping.
the alarm stage
The alarm stage is a physiological stage of stress response, not a coping act.
learned helplessness
Learned helplessness is passivity after uncontrollable stress, not calming oneself.
questions.x: Meditation after an unavoidable loss manages emotional distress rather than changing the situation, which is emotion-focused coping. Trap: Believing emotion-focused coping is always maladaptive.

questions.q: Self-determination theory identifies three basic psychological needs:
o: safety, love, esteem
Safety, love, and esteem are levels in Maslow's hierarchy.
drive, incentive, arousal
Drive, incentive, and arousal are separate motivation theories.
autonomy, competence, and relatedness
Correct: Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster intrinsic motivation.
extrinsic, intrinsic, amotivation
Extrinsic, intrinsic, and amotivation are types of motivation, not needs.
questions.x: Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the basic needs that foster intrinsic motivation. Trap: Confusing self-determination theory's three needs with the levels of Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.q: Bilateral removal of the temporal lobes including the amygdala in monkeys produced:
o: heightened aggression and fear
Fear and aggression are reduced, not heightened.
loss of vision
Vision is not lost, though objects are not recognized for what they are.
inability to form new declarative memories only
The defining features are emotional and behavioral, not a memory-only deficit.
tameness, loss of fear, and hyperorality
Correct: Bilateral temporal lobe removal including the amygdala produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality, and hypersexuality.
questions.x: Bilateral temporal lobe removal including the amygdala produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality, and hypersexuality. Trap: Assuming amygdala damage increases fear and aggression.

questions.q: Researchers compare a trait's concordance in monozygotic twins reared apart with that in dizygotic twins reared together. Higher concordance in the monozygotic pairs would most directly suggest that:
o: genetic factors contribute to variation in the trait
Correct: MZ twins share nearly all their genes, so greater concordance than DZ twins, even when reared apart, implicates genetic influence on the trait.
shared family environment is the sole determinant of the trait
Shared family environment cannot explain similarity in twins raised apart, and it is equal-ish for DZ twins reared together.
the trait is fully determined by genes with no environmental input
MZ concordance below 100% would still show environmental input, so full genetic determination is not implied.
the trait arises from random developmental error
Random developmental error would not produce systematically higher concordance in genetically identical pairs.
questions.x: MZ twins share nearly all their genes, so greater concordance than DZ twins, even when reared apart, implicates genetic influence on the trait. Trap: Equating high heritability with complete genetic determination.

questions.q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes that positive symptoms such as hallucinations result from:
o: deficient acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions
Deficient acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions describes myasthenia-type weakness, not psychosis.
loss of GABA-mediated inhibition in the spinal cord
Loss of spinal GABA inhibition relates to spasticity or tetanus-like effects, not hallucinations.
excess dopamine activity in mesolimbic pathways
Correct: The dopamine hypothesis ties positive symptoms like hallucinations to overactivity of dopamine in mesolimbic pathways, and antipsychotics work by blocking D2 receptors.
depleted serotonin in the raphe nuclei only
Depleted serotonin in the raphe nuclei is linked to depression and is not the dopamine hypothesis.
questions.x: The dopamine hypothesis ties positive symptoms like hallucinations to overactivity of dopamine in mesolimbic pathways, and antipsychotics work by blocking D2 receptors. Trap: Confusing the dopamine deficit in Parkinson disease with the excess in schizophrenia.

questions.q: Participants injected with epinephrine reported anger or euphoria depending on a confederate's behavior. This supports which theory?
o: James-Lange theory, in which arousal alone defines the emotion
James-Lange has no labeling step and would predict the same emotion regardless of the confederate.
Two-factor theory, in which arousal is cognitively labeled
Correct: Two-factor theory holds that emotion arises from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from context, as the confederate's behavior supplied here.
Cannon-Bard theory, in which emotion precedes arousal
Cannon-Bard claims simultaneity, not emotion preceding arousal, and ignores situational labeling.
the facial feedback hypothesis only
Facial feedback concerns facial expression influencing emotion, not injected arousal and social cues.
questions.x: Two-factor theory holds that emotion arises from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from context, as the confederate's behavior supplied here. Trap: Ignoring the role of the situational cue.

questions.q: A person who has two or more distinct personality states and gaps in memory for everyday events is most likely diagnosed with:
o: dissociative identity disorder
Correct: Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct identities or personality states and amnesia beyond ordinary forgetting.
borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder features unstable relationships, self-image, and mood, not distinct identities.
schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder involving hallucinations and delusions, not split identities.
schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid personality disorder involves detachment and limited emotional expression, not identity fragmentation.
questions.x: Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct identities or personality states and amnesia beyond ordinary forgetting. Trap: Equating schizophrenia with split personality.

questions.q: A person who repeatedly lies, violates others' rights, and shows no remorse most likely has:
o: antisocial personality disorder
Correct: Antisocial personality disorder involves a pervasive pattern of deceit, disregard for others' rights, and lack of remorse.
avoidant personality disorder
Avoidant personality disorder involves social inhibition and fear of rejection.
dependent personality disorder
Dependent personality disorder involves an excessive need to be cared for and submissiveness.
obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder involves perfectionism and rigid control, not rights violations.
questions.x: Antisocial personality disorder involves a pervasive pattern of deceit, disregard for others' rights, and lack of remorse. Trap: Confusing antisocial personality disorder with avoidant or dependent patterns because all are personality disorders.

questions.q: A group of moderately cautious investors becomes much more cautious after discussion. This is:
o: groupthink
Groupthink involves suppressed dissent and flawed decisions, not a shift in initial leaning.
group polarization
Correct: Group polarization is the intensification of the group's initial average leaning after discussion, so moderately cautious members become much more cautious.
conformity to an external norm
Conformity to an external norm involves adopting an outside standard, not intensifying the group's own leaning.
social loafing
Social loafing is reduced effort in groups and does not shift attitudes.
questions.x: Group polarization is the intensification of the group's initial average leaning after discussion, so moderately cautious members become much more cautious. Trap: Assuming groups always move to moderate positions.

questions.q: Individuals boost self-esteem by viewing their own group more favorably than other groups. This reflects:
o: the contact hypothesis
The contact hypothesis addresses conditions under which intergroup contact reduces prejudice.
social identity theory with ingroup bias
Correct: Social identity theory holds that group membership contributes to self-concept, so people boost self-esteem through ingroup bias, favoring their own group.
the Barnum effect
The Barnum effect is accepting vague, general personality descriptions as personally accurate.
self-perception theory
Self-perception theory says people infer their attitudes from observing their own behavior.
questions.x: Social identity theory holds that group membership contributes to self-concept, so people boost self-esteem through ingroup bias, favoring their own group. Trap: Overlooking that group membership feeds self-esteem.

questions.q: According to Cooley, a person develops a self-concept by:
o: internalizing instinctual drives
Internalizing instinctual drives is Freud's id-based framework, not Cooley's.
comparing to an ideal self only
Comparing to an ideal self only is Rogers's or Higgins's self-discrepancy idea, not social-mirror judgment.
imagining how others perceive and judge them
Correct: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that the self-concept arises from imagining how others perceive and judge us.
observing physiological arousal
Observing one's own physiological arousal relates to emotion theories such as James-Lange or Schachter-Singer.
questions.x: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that the self-concept arises from imagining how others perceive and judge us. Trap: Mixing Cooley's imagined social judgment with Mead's stage-based role-taking theory.

questions.q: A job candidate dresses carefully and emphasizes strengths to create a favorable image. This is:
o: fundamental attribution error
Fundamental attribution error is overweighting dispositions in judging others' behavior.
impression management
Correct: Impression management is deliberately controlling how others perceive us, such as dressing carefully and emphasizing strengths.
stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is impaired performance from fear of confirming a negative stereotype.
deindividuation
Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in anonymous groups, the opposite of deliberate self-presentation.
questions.x: Impression management is deliberately controlling how others perceive us, such as dressing carefully and emphasizing strengths. Trap: Thinking impression management only means lying rather than controlling how one is perceived.

questions.q: A manager assumes a very attractive employee is also competent and honest. This is the:
o: fundamental attribution error
Fundamental attribution error concerns explaining behavior by disposition over situation.
just-world hypothesis
The just-world hypothesis is assuming people get what they deserve.
halo effect
Correct: The halo effect is letting one positive trait, such as attractiveness, lead to positive assumptions about other traits like competence and honesty.
self-serving bias
Self-serving bias is attributing one's own successes to self and failures to circumstances.
questions.x: The halo effect is letting one positive trait, such as attractiveness, lead to positive assumptions about other traits like competence and honesty. Trap: Confusing the halo effect with stereotyping, though it spreads one trait to others for an individual.

questions.q: Parents praising boys for assertiveness and girls for helpfulness illustrates:
o: gender role socialization via reinforcement
Correct: Differential reinforcement by parents, praising boys for assertiveness and girls for helpfulness, shapes gender role learning (socialization).
genetic essentialism
Genetic essentialism treats gender differences as innate, not shaped by praise.
classical conditioning of gender
Classical conditioning of gender involves stimulus pairing, not selective praise as operant reinforcement.
stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is performance impairment when a negative stereotype is salient.
questions.x: Differential reinforcement by parents, praising boys for assertiveness and girls for helpfulness, shapes gender role learning (socialization). Trap: Treating gender roles as innate rather than learned through differential reinforcement.

questions.q: Slot machines pay out after unpredictable numbers of pulls, producing persistent responding. This is:
o: fixed-ratio schedule
A fixed-ratio schedule produces bursts with pauses after reinforcement.
fixed-interval schedule
A fixed-interval schedule gives scalloped responding that accelerates before the predictable reward time.
variable-interval schedule
A variable-interval schedule depends on unpredictable time rather than number of pulls, and gives slower steady rates.
variable-ratio schedule
Correct: A variable-ratio schedule reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses, yielding high, steady rates and strong resistance to extinction, as in slot machines.
questions.x: A variable-ratio schedule reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses, yielding high, steady rates and strong resistance to extinction, as in slot machines. Trap: Confusing ratio schedules, based on responses, with interval schedules, based on time.

questions.q: A teenager begins to see herself as artistic because teachers and classmates consistently describe her that way and praise her drawings. Which concept best explains how her self-view developed?
o: Cooley's looking-glass self
Correct: Cooley holds that self-concept arises from imagining how others perceive and judge us.
Freud's reaction formation
Reaction formation is a defense mechanism expressing the opposite of an unacceptable impulse.
Bandura's self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to perform a task, not an inferred reflection of others' views.
Erikson's moratorium
Moratorium is a (Marcia) status of exploring without commitment, not a process of absorbing others' appraisals.
questions.x: Cooley holds that self-concept arises from imagining how others perceive and judge us. Trap: Confusing the looking-glass self with Mead's role-taking stages because both are symbolic interactionist ideas.

questions.q: A 5-year-old plays 'doctor,' acting out how a doctor speaks to a patient, but cannot yet coordinate several roles at once the way players on a team must. Which stage in Mead's theory is this?
o: Preparatory stage
The preparatory stage is imitation without understanding roles, earlier than this.
Play stage
Correct: In the play stage children take on the roles of specific significant others one at a time.
Game stage
The game stage requires tracking multiple roles at once and a generalized other.
Formal operational stage
This is a Piaget stage, not part of Mead's theory.
questions.x: In the play stage children take on the roles of specific significant others one at a time. Trap: Choosing the game stage because the child is playing.

questions.q: After failing an exam, a student concludes, 'The test was unfair and the professor dislikes me.' A student who thinks this way across many situations most likely has:
o: an internal locus of control
An internal locus attributes outcomes to one's own effort and ability.
an external locus of control
Correct: Attributing outcomes to luck, others, or circumstances is an external locus of control.
high self-efficacy
High self-efficacy involves belief in one's ability to affect outcomes.
a self-discrepancy between actual and ideal self
Nothing in the scenario compares actual and ideal selves.
questions.x: Attributing outcomes to luck, others, or circumstances is an external locus of control. Trap: Treating blame of others as a sign of high self-esteem rather than an external locus.

questions.q: Two students interpret the same handshake differently: one as respect, the other as a challenge. Which theory best emphasizes this variability?
o: Structural functionalism
Structural functionalism is macro-level and looks at how structures sustain society.
Symbolic interactionism
